title: Azure Fundamentals
subtitle: Climb the money ladder — one Azure question per grade level

options: A Microsoft antivirus software suite installed on your PC
Microsoft's public cloud platform delivering computing services over the internet
A private data center that only government agencies can use
Microsoft's brand name for its line of Surface laptops
questions.note: Azure is Microsoft's public cloud — a global network of datacenters delivering compute, storage, networking, and more over the internet on a pay-as-you-go model.

explain.correct: Microsoft Azure is a public cloud platform that delivers over 200 products and services — compute, storage, networking, AI, and more — over the internet from Microsoft-owned global datacenters.
wrong: Azure is not antivirus software. Microsoft Defender is Microsoft's security/antivirus product family.
Azure is a public cloud, not a government-only private facility. Azure Government is a separate sovereign cloud for US government use, but Azure itself is public.
Azure has nothing to do with Surface hardware. Surface is Microsoft's PC and tablet product line.

questions.q: A company rents virtual machines from Azure and is responsible for installing and patching the operating system itself. Which cloud service model does this represent?
options: Software as a Service (SaaS)
Platform as a Service (PaaS)
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
Function as a Service (FaaS)
questions.note: IaaS gives you raw infrastructure (VMs, networking, storage). You manage the OS and above; the cloud provider manages the physical hardware. Azure Virtual Machines is the canonical IaaS example.

explain.correct: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) provides virtualized hardware — compute, networking, and storage. The customer controls the OS, middleware, and applications. Azure Virtual Machines is the primary IaaS offering.
wrong: SaaS delivers fully managed applications over the internet (e.g., Microsoft 365). The customer only manages data and user access — no OS or runtime responsibility.
PaaS provides a managed platform for building apps (e.g., Azure App Service). Microsoft manages the OS and runtime; the customer manages the application and data.
FaaS (e.g., Azure Functions) is a serverless model — a subset of PaaS. The provider manages everything down to the runtime; you only supply the function code.

questions.q: A developer wants to run a small piece of code only when an HTTP request arrives, with no server to provision or maintain. Which Azure compute service is the best fit?
options: Azure Virtual Machines
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
Azure App Service
Azure Functions
questions.note: Azure Functions is Azure's serverless compute offering — code executes in response to triggers (HTTP, timer, queue message) and you pay only for execution time. No VM or container cluster to manage.

explain.correct: Azure Functions is a serverless (event-driven) compute service. Code runs on-demand in response to triggers such as HTTP requests, timers, or queue messages. There is no infrastructure to provision or patch.
wrong: Azure Virtual Machines require you to provision, configure, and maintain the OS — the opposite of serverless. You pay whether the VM is idle or busy.
Azure Kubernetes Service manages containerized workloads across a cluster of nodes. It is powerful but requires container packaging and cluster management — far more overhead than needed here.

App Service is a PaaS platform for hosting continuously-running web applications and REST APIs; unlike Azure Functions it is not event-triggered and not serverless -- the app runs whether or not requests arrive.

questions.q: When you create an Azure resource such as a virtual machine, what does selecting a "region" determine?
options: Which Microsoft support tier the resource is assigned to
The physical geographic location of the datacenters where the resource will be hosted
The subscription billing currency for that resource
The programming language runtime available to the resource
questions.note: An Azure region is a set of datacenters deployed within a latency-defined perimeter and connected via a dedicated low-latency network. Every Azure resource is deployed to exactly one region.

explain.correct: A region represents one or more datacenters located in the same geographic area (e.g., East US, West Europe). Choosing a region determines where your resource physically runs, which affects latency, data residency, and feature availability.
wrong: Support tiers (Basic, Developer, Standard, Professional Direct) are set at the subscription level and are independent of region selection.
Billing currency is determined by your Azure account's billing profile and country/region of enrollment — not by which Azure region a resource is deployed to.
Runtime availability (e.g., .NET, Node.js, Python on App Service) is a feature of the service itself, not a property of the Azure region.

questions.q: An organization needs its Azure virtual machines to remain online even if a single datacenter within a region suffers a complete power failure. Which feature should they use?
options: Azure Region Pairs
Azure Availability Sets
Azure Availability Zones
Azure Site Recovery
questions.note: Availability Zones are physically separate datacenters within the same Azure region — each with independent power, cooling, and networking. Spreading VMs across zones protects against a single-datacenter failure.

explain.correct: Availability Zones are physically distinct datacenter buildings within one region, each with their own independent power, cooling, and network feeds. Deploying resources across at least two zones means a single-datacenter outage does not take down all instances.
wrong: Region Pairs are two separate Azure regions paired for regional disaster recovery (e.g., East US paired with West US). They protect against full-region failures, not single-datacenter failures within a region.

Availability Sets spread VMs across fault domains and update domains within a single datacenter (not across physically separate buildings), offering protection against hardware rack failures and planned maintenance windows — but not full datacenter outages.

Azure Site Recovery is a disaster recovery orchestration service that replicates workloads to a secondary region. It is a DR tool, not a high-availability mechanism for surviving a single-datacenter failure transparently.

questions.q: A cloud administrator deletes an Azure Resource Group named "Prod-RG" that contains 12 virtual machines, 3 storage accounts, and a virtual network. What happens to those resources?
options: The resources are moved to a default "Recycle" resource group and can be restored within 30 days
Only unattached resources (storage accounts, VNet) are deleted; running VMs are preserved
All 12 VMs, 3 storage accounts, and the virtual network are permanently deleted along with the resource group
The deletion is blocked until each resource is individually stopped and de-allocated
questions.note: Deleting a Resource Group is a cascade-delete operation — every resource contained in the group is permanently destroyed. There is no automatic recovery bin for resource groups.

explain.correct: In Azure, the Resource Group is a logical container. Deleting the Resource Group triggers a cascade-delete of every resource inside it — VMs, storage accounts, virtual networks, and all other contained resources are permanently deleted. There is no built-in undo.
wrong: Azure has no "Recycle" resource group or 30-day recovery bin for resource group deletions. Soft-delete exists for specific services (e.g., Azure Key Vault, Blob Storage with soft-delete enabled) but not for resource groups as a whole.
Resource Group deletion does not distinguish between running and stopped resources, or between attached and unattached resources. All contained resources are deleted regardless of their state.
Azure does not block resource group deletion based on individual resource states. Once you confirm the deletion prompt, all resources in the group are queued for permanent removal.

questions.q: Which Microsoft service provides cloud-based identity and access management for Azure resources, supports multi-factor authentication, and replaces the older name "Azure Active Directory"?
options: Microsoft Entra ID
Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)
Microsoft Identity Manager (MIM)
Azure Key Vault
questions.note: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory / Azure AD) is Microsoft's cloud identity platform. It handles authentication, MFA, Conditional Access, and RBAC role assignments for Azure and Microsoft 365.

explain.correct: Microsoft Entra ID is the cloud-native identity and access management service formerly known as Azure Active Directory (Azure AD). It provides user authentication, multi-factor authentication (MFA), Conditional Access policies, and role-based access control (RBAC) for Azure resources and Microsoft 365.
wrong: Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is the traditional on-premises directory service that runs on Windows Server. It is not a cloud service and is separate from Microsoft Entra ID, though they can be synchronized via Microsoft Entra Connect.
Microsoft Identity Manager (MIM) is an on-premises identity lifecycle and synchronization tool — it is not the primary cloud identity platform for Azure.
Azure Key Vault is a service for storing and managing secrets, encryption keys, and certificates. It is a security service, not an identity provider or access management platform.

questions.q: A company stores large video files in Azure Blob Storage. The files are accessed multiple times per day for the first 30 days after creation, then rarely accessed for the next 11 months. Which Blob access tier strategy minimizes total cost?
options: Store all files in the Hot tier permanently to avoid retrieval fees
Store all files in the Archive tier immediately to minimize storage cost
Start files in the Hot tier, then move them to the Cool tier after 30 days
Store all files in the Cool tier from the beginning since retrieval fees are low
questions.note: Hot tier has low access cost but high storage cost; Cool tier has lower storage cost but higher per-GB retrieval fees and a 30-day minimum storage period. Lifecycle management policies automate tier transitions.

explain.correct: Hot tier is optimized for frequently accessed data — low access cost, higher storage price. Cool tier is optimized for infrequently accessed data held at least 30 days — lower storage price but higher retrieval cost. Moving files to Cool after the active period minimizes total cost by matching tier to access pattern.
wrong: Keeping all files in the Hot tier permanently wastes money during the 11 months of rare access, because Hot has higher per-GB storage costs compared to Cool or Archive.

Immediately archiving files incurs a mandatory 180-day minimum storage period and high retrieval latency (up to 15 hours for standard rehydration). Accessing archived files frequently in the first 30 days would result in very high retrieval costs.

Storing files in Cool from creation means paying higher retrieval costs during the first 30 days of frequent access, which outweighs the storage savings compared to using Hot during the active period.

questions.q: An organization in the East US region needs their Azure storage data to survive the failure of an entire Azure region — not just a single datacenter or zone. Which redundancy option satisfies this requirement at the lowest complexity?
options: Locally Redundant Storage (LRS) — three copies within a single datacenter
Zone-Redundant Storage (ZRS) — copies across three Availability Zones in the same region
Geo-Redundant Storage (GRS) -- LRS copies within the primary region, plus asynchronous replication to a paired secondary region
Premium SSD — NVMe storage with high IOPS and low latency
questions.note: GRS replicates data three times in the primary region (like LRS) and then asynchronously replicates to a paired secondary region (e.g., East US pairs with West US), protecting against full-region failures.

explain.correct: Geo-Redundant Storage (GRS) maintains three copies in the primary region using LRS and asynchronously replicates to a geographically paired secondary region. This protects against a full regional outage. The paired region for East US is West US.
wrong: Locally Redundant Storage (LRS) keeps three copies within a single datacenter in one region. A datacenter or regional failure would destroy all copies — it provides no protection against region-level failures.

Zone-Redundant Storage (ZRS) replicates data synchronously across three Availability Zones within the same region. It protects against single-datacenter failures but does NOT protect against the failure of an entire Azure region, since all zones are in the same geographic area.
Premium SSD is a disk performance tier for Azure managed disks, not a storage redundancy option. It refers to IOPS and latency characteristics, not data durability or geographic replication.

questions.q: A security team wants to ensure that no Azure resource in their subscription can be created without a specific "CostCenter" tag, and that no one — including subscription owners — can create resources in regions outside North America. Which Azure governance tool enforces these WHAT rules on resource creation?
options: Azure Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) — assign the Reader role to prevent unauthorized creations
Azure Resource Locks — apply a ReadOnly lock at the subscription level
Azure Policy — assign policy definitions with Deny effects targeting the required tag and allowed regions
Microsoft Entra ID Conditional Access — block access tokens for requests originating outside North America
questions.note: Azure Policy controls WHAT resources can look like — it enforces organizational rules (require tags, restrict regions, mandate SKUs) using Deny, Audit, and Modify effects. RBAC controls WHO can take action. These are complementary, not interchangeable.

explain.correct: Azure Policy is the governance tool that defines and enforces rules about WHAT resources can be created or configured. Policy definitions with the Deny effect will block non-compliant resource creation outright — for example, requiring the CostCenter tag or restricting deployments to specific Azure regions. Policies inherit downward through the Management Group > Subscription > Resource Group hierarchy.
wrong: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) determines WHO can perform actions — it grants or denies permissions to identities (users, groups, service principals). It cannot enforce resource properties like required tags or restrict which Azure regions are used by authorized users.

Resource Locks (CanNotDelete and ReadOnly) prevent accidental modification or deletion of existing resources. A ReadOnly lock does not block new resource creation with missing tags, and it cannot restrict deployment regions.

Microsoft Entra ID Conditional Access controls how and from where users authenticate — it can block sign-ins from certain locations or devices. It does not govern Azure resource creation policies such as required tags or allowed deployment regions.

questions.q: An IT director wants to estimate how much money the company would save by migrating their on-premises server workloads to Azure, factoring in current hardware, power, cooling, and IT labor costs. Which Azure tool is designed for this specific analysis?
options: Azure Pricing Calculator — configure Azure services and see their estimated monthly cost
Azure Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) Calculator — compare on-premises costs against projected Azure costs
Microsoft Cost Management — view and analyze actual Azure spending after resources are deployed
Azure Advisor — receive personalized recommendations across cost, security, reliability, and performance
questions.note: The TCO Calculator is a pre-sales/planning tool for on-premises-to-Azure migration decisions. The Pricing Calculator estimates Azure service costs before deployment. Cost Management shows actual post-deployment spending. Azure Advisor analyzes live deployments.

explain.correct: The Azure Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) Calculator is specifically designed for migration planning. You input your current on-premises workloads — servers, databases, storage, networking — and it estimates your existing total cost (hardware, power, cooling, data center space, IT labor) versus the projected Azure cost, producing a side-by-side comparison to quantify migration savings.
wrong: The Azure Pricing Calculator lets you select and configure Azure services to estimate what those services would cost per month in Azure. It does not model or compare on-premises costs — it only covers Azure-side pricing.

Microsoft Cost Management (formerly Azure Cost Management + Billing) analyzes ACTUAL spending on deployed Azure resources. It is a post-deployment monitoring and optimization tool, not a pre-migration planning calculator.

Azure Advisor analyzes your existing Azure environment and makes recommendations across five pillars: Cost, Security, Reliability, Operational Excellence, and Performance. It requires live Azure resources to analyze and does not compare on-premises costs to Azure.
